facts.text: Hydrogen is the lightest element and makes up about 75% of all matter in the universe — stars like our Sun are mostly hydrogen.
When hydrogen burns, the only thing it produces is water, making it one of the cleanest fuels possible.
There is more hydrogen in a glass of water than in a glass of pure hydrogen gas!
The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen, which caused it to catch fire spectacularly in 1937.

image_caption: Helium glowing orange-red in a discharge tube

facts.text: Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth — its name comes from 'Helios', the Greek god of the Sun.
Helium is so light that if you release a helium balloon, it flies into space and is gone forever.
Unlike every other substance, liquid helium never freezes solid — it stays liquid all the way down to absolute zero.
Breathing helium makes your voice squeaky because sound travels faster through it than through regular air.

facts.text: Carbon is the basis of all life — every living thing on Earth is built from carbon chains.
Diamond and graphite (pencil 'lead') are both made of pure carbon, just arranged differently.
Scientists use radioactive carbon-14 to calculate the age of ancient bones and fossils — a technique called carbon dating.
A single carbon atom can bond to four other atoms at once, which is why carbon can build millions of different molecules.

facts.text: Oxygen makes up 21% of the air we breathe, and liquid oxygen is a beautiful pale blue colour.
Without oxygen, fire cannot burn — it needs oxygen to keep going.
Your blood looks red because the iron in haemoglobin carries oxygen molecules around your body.
Oxygen was discovered in 1774 and was first called 'dephlogisticated air' — a name that thankfully did not stick.

facts.text: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air around you, but your body cannot use it directly from the air.
Liquid nitrogen is so cold (−196°C) that it instantly freezes anything it touches.
Plants need nitrogen to grow, which is why farmers spread nitrogen-rich fertilisers on their fields.
Lightning bolts convert nitrogen gas into a form that dissolves in rain, giving plants a natural fertiliser from the sky.

facts.text: Gold never rusts or tarnishes — a gold coin buried 3,000 years ago still shines as brightly as the day it was made.
All the gold ever mined in human history would fit inside about 3.5 Olympic swimming pools.
Gold is so stretchy that 1 gram can be hammered into a sheet 1 square metre wide, thinner than a human hair.
Your smartphone contains tiny amounts of gold in its circuit board because gold conducts electricity reliably without corroding.

facts.text: Silver conducts electricity better than any other metal, though gold is more commonly used in electronics because silver tarnishes.
Before refrigerators, people put silver coins in milk to keep it fresh — silver ions kill bacteria.
Film photography worked by exposing silver compounds to light, which turned dark where light hit them — creating the image.
The country Argentina is named after silver — early Spanish explorers believed the region was filled with silver deposits.

facts.text: Iron is the most common element in the entire Earth by mass — the core of our planet is a giant ball of solid and liquid iron.
Your blood is red because of iron — the iron in haemoglobin grabs oxygen in your lungs and carries it to every cell in your body.
The Iron Age began around 1200 BC when humans discovered how to smelt iron, allowing them to make far stronger tools than bronze.
Iron is the only everyday element you can pick up with a magnet.

image_caption: Native copper specimen

compounds.name: Cuprite

facts.text: The Statue of Liberty is made of copper — its famous green colour developed slowly as the copper reacted with air and rain over decades.
Copper was one of the first metals ever used by humans, more than 10,000 years ago.
Copper kills bacteria — that is why door handles and railings in many hospitals are made of copper to reduce germ spreading.
Almost all the electric wires in your home are made of copper because it conducts electricity nearly as well as silver but costs far less.

facts.text: The word 'plumber' comes from plumbum — the Romans used lead pipes to carry water across their cities.
Lead is so soft and dense that you can scratch it with your fingernail, yet it blocks X-rays and radiation.
Lead was once added to paint and petrol, but was banned when scientists discovered it causes serious brain damage.
A typical car battery contains about 8 kg of lead — cars still use lead-acid batteries to start the engine.

compounds.name: Washing soda

compounds.name: Sodium fluoride

facts.text: Pure sodium explodes violently when it touches water, releasing hydrogen gas and a huge burst of heat.
Your nerves use sodium ions to send electrical signals — without sodium you could not feel, move, or think.
Salt was so valuable in ancient Rome that soldiers were sometimes paid in it — that is where the word 'salary' comes from.
The orange glow of old street lamps comes from sodium — sodium atoms produce a brilliant orange-yellow light when heated.

image_caption: Potassium metal pearls stored in paraffin oil

compounds.name: Potassium chloride

compounds.name: Potassium hydroxide

compounds.name: Potassium nitrate

compounds.name: Potash
compounds.use: Used in making glass and soap for centuries

compounds.name: Potassium iodide
compounds.use: Added to table salt to prevent iodine deficiency

facts.text: Bananas contain potassium, which helps your muscles work properly — including the most important one, your heart.
Potassium reacts even more violently with water than sodium, skidding across the surface while burning with a lilac flame.
Your body needs potassium and sodium together to control the balance of fluids inside and outside every cell.
Gunpowder contains potassium nitrate — it has been used in weapons and fireworks for over a thousand years.

facts.text: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in your body — 99% of it lives in your bones and teeth, making them hard.
Seashells, chalk, marble, and limestone cliffs are all made of exactly the same compound: calcium carbonate.
Milk is rich in calcium because baby animals need it to build strong bones quickly while they are growing.
Calcium fizzes slowly when you drop it in water, releasing hydrogen gas bubbles — similar to sodium but much calmer.

compounds.name: Polyvinyl chloride

compounds.name: Chloroform

facts.text: Swimming pools smell of chlorine because it is added to kill harmful bacteria — without it, pools would be dangerous to swim in.
The chlorine in table salt is completely harmless — chlorine is only dangerous as a pure gas.
Chlorine gas was used as a chemical weapon in World War I — soldiers described its smell as a mix of pineapple and pepper.
Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid to digest food — the same type of acid used to dissolve metals in chemistry labs.

compounds.name: Sulphur hexafluoride

facts.text: Fluorine is the most reactive element on the periodic table — it attacks almost every substance, including glass and most metals.
Fluoride is added to toothpaste and tap water in many countries because it makes tooth enamel much harder and more resistant to decay.
Teflon, the non-stick coating on frying pans, contains fluorine — it is one of the very few materials that fluorine cannot destroy.
Fluorine gas is so dangerous that even a tiny leak can be fatal — it is one of the most carefully handled substances in chemistry.

compounds.name: Lithium cobalt oxide

compounds.name: Lithium chloride

facts.text: Lithium is so light it can float on water — and it's the lightest of all metals, lighter than most woods!
Every rechargeable phone, laptop, and electric car battery relies on lithium to store energy.
Lithium burns with a brilliant crimson-red flame, which is why it's used in some fireworks and flares.
Lithium was one of the three elements created in the Big Bang — along with hydrogen and helium — making it almost as old as the universe itself.

compounds.name: Boric acid

facts.text: Crystalline boron is one of the hardest elements — almost as hard as diamond, and it can scratch most metals.
Boron is used in the control rods of nuclear reactors because it absorbs neutrons and keeps chain reactions in check.
The mineral borax (a boron compound) has been mined for over 4,000 years and was used by ancient goldsmiths to clean and join metals.
Boron fibres are stronger than steel by weight and are woven into high-performance aircraft parts and sports equipment.

image_caption: Neon glowing its iconic orange-red colour inside a glass discharge tube.

facts.text: The famous glow of 'neon signs' is actually neon — the orange-red colour is pure neon, while other colours use different gases.
Neon is the fourth most abundant element in the universe but is extremely rare on Earth — most escaped into space long ago.
Neon was discovered in 1898, just a few weeks after krypton, when scientists cooled air until it turned liquid and boiled off the different gases one by one.
Like all noble gases, neon refuses to react with anything — its outer electron shell is completely full and perfectly satisfied.

compounds.name: Epsom salt

compounds.name: Milk of magnesia
compounds.use: A common medicine for indigestion and constipation

compounds.name: Magnesium chloride
compounds.use: Sprinkled on icy roads to melt ice in winter

facts.text: Magnesium burns with an incredibly bright white flame — so bright it was used in old camera flash bulbs and emergency flares.
Every green plant on Earth owes its colour to magnesium — it sits right at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule.
Magnesium is the eighth most abundant element in Earth's crust and is found in over 60 different minerals.
Racing cars, aircraft, and laptops use magnesium alloys because magnesium is two-thirds lighter than aluminium but still very strong.

compounds.name: Aluminium chloride

compounds.name: Alum

facts.text: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust — about 8% of all rocks and soil contain it.
In the 1800s, aluminium was more precious than gold because it was so hard to extract; the tip of the Washington Monument is capped with aluminium.
A recycled aluminium can uses 95% less energy to make than a brand-new one — recycling aluminium really does make a huge difference.
Aluminium is so light that a cube the size of a football only weighs about as much as a bag of sugar.

compounds.name: Silicon nitride

facts.text: Silicon is the foundation of modern computers — tiny silicon chips smaller than your fingernail can contain billions of transistors.
Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 28% of it — mostly as sand and quartz.
Sand (silicon dioxide) can be transformed into glass by melting it — your window and phone screen both started life as sand.
Silicon Valley in California got its name because so many computer chip companies set up there in the 1970s and 80s.

compounds.name: Adenosine triphosphate

facts.text: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark — this eerie glow gave it its name, from the Greek word for 'light-bearing'.
Phosphorus is absolutely essential for life — it forms the backbone of DNA and is the 'P' in ATP, the energy currency of every living cell.
Phosphorus was first isolated in 1669 by a German alchemist boiling down enormous quantities of urine, hoping to find gold — he got a glowing substance instead.
The 'strike anywhere' matches work because they contain red phosphorus, which ignites with just a little friction and heat.

facts.text: Sulfur is the reason rotten eggs smell so horrible — bacteria release tiny amounts of hydrogen sulfide gas as they break down proteins.
Ancient peoples called sulfur 'brimstone' and it appears in the Bible — the fires of hell were imagined to burn with its choking smell.
Sulfur is bright yellow and is found in huge deposits around volcanoes — some craters look like they are filled with powdered sunshine.
Your body contains about 140 grams of sulfur — it's found in two essential amino acids that build your proteins and hair.

image_caption: Argon glowing violet-purple inside a glass discharge tube when electricity passes through it.

facts.text: Argon makes up about 1% of the air you breathe — every breath you take contains more argon than carbon dioxide.
Argon gets its name from the Greek word 'argos', meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive', because it refuses to react with almost anything.
Argon is pumped between the panes of double-glazed windows because it conducts heat poorly, keeping homes warmer in winter.
Museum conservators fill display cases with argon to protect ancient documents and artefacts, because argon won't react with or damage them.

compounds.name: Zinc sulfide

compounds.name: Zinc chloride
compounds.use: Used in dry-cell batteries and as a flux for soldering metals

facts.text: Zinc is used to coat steel in a process called galvanising — the zinc layer rusts away first, sacrificing itself to protect the steel underneath.
Your body needs zinc to heal wounds, fight infections, and even to taste and smell properly — it's in many cold and flu remedies.
Brass, one of the most useful alloys in history (used in trumpets, door handles, and old coins), is simply copper mixed with zinc.
Most of the 'copper' one-cent coins produced in the USA since 1983 are actually 97.5% zinc with just a thin copper coating.

compounds.name: Silver bromide

compounds.name: Dibromomethane

compounds.name: Potassium bromide
compounds.use: Historically used as a sedative and anti-seizure medicine

facts.text: Bromine is one of only two elements that is a liquid at room temperature (the other is mercury) — it's a dark reddish-brown, fuming liquid.
Bromine has a horrible, choking smell — its name comes from the Greek word 'bromos', meaning 'stench'.
The ancient Phoenicians extracted a purple dye called Tyrian purple from sea snails; it gets its colour from a bromine-containing molecule and was so expensive it was reserved for royalty.
Bromine compounds were once used as flame retardants in electronics and furniture foam, though many have since been phased out due to environmental concerns.

image_caption: Krypton glowing white inside a glass discharge tube.

facts.text: Krypton's name comes from the Greek word 'kryptos', meaning 'hidden' — the same root as Superman's home planet Krypton!
From 1960 to 1983, the official definition of one metre was based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by krypton-86 atoms.
Krypton is used in high-powered camera flash lamps and airport runway lights because it produces an extremely bright, white light.
Krypton was discovered in 1898 by boiling down liquid air — there was so little of it that it took processing enormous amounts of air to collect just a tiny sample.

image_caption: Alpha tin (grey powder, left) and beta tin (shiny metal, right) — two very different forms of the same element.

compounds.name: Tin chloride
compounds.use: Used as a food preservative and as a reducing agent in chemistry

compounds.name: Tin hydroxide
compounds.use: Used in some dental cements and as a mordant in dyeing fabric

compounds.name: Tin phosphate
compounds.use: Used in corrosion-resistant coatings for metal surfaces

facts.text: Tin has been used by humans for over 5,000 years — bronze (tin + copper) was so important it defined an entire age of human history, the Bronze Age.

In very cold weather, tin slowly crumbles into grey powder in a process called 'tin pest' — this may have contributed to the failure of Napoleon's army in the Russian winter, as tin buttons on uniforms disintegrated.
Tin's chemical symbol Sn comes from its Latin name 'Stannum' — and the element stannum gave its name to the English county Cornwall, once a major tin-mining region.
The 'tin can' used for food preservation since the 1800s is actually a steel can with only a thin tin coating — but tin resists corrosion well enough to keep food safe for years.

image_caption: A sample of solid iodine showing its lustrous dark grey-black crystalline form.

compounds.name: Potassium iodide
compounds.use: Added to table salt to prevent iodine deficiency and thyroid disease

compounds.name: Iodine solution
compounds.use: Used as an antiseptic to clean wounds and kill bacteria

compounds.name: Sodium iodate
compounds.use: Used to iodise salt and as a disinfectant in water treatment

compounds.name: Silver iodide
compounds.use: Used in cloud seeding to encourage rainfall and in some photographic films

facts.text: When solid iodine is heated, it skips the liquid phase entirely and turns straight into a beautiful purple-violet vapour — a process called sublimation.
Iodine is essential for your thyroid gland, which controls your growth and metabolism — a lack of iodine causes a swelling of the throat called a goitre.
The brown antiseptic liquid used to clean cuts is an iodine solution — iodine kills bacteria by attacking their proteins and DNA.
Your body contains only about 15–20 milligrams of iodine, but without it you cannot make the hormones that control your body's energy use.

image_caption: Xenon glowing blue-white inside a glass discharge tube.

facts.text: Xenon was the first noble gas ever made into a chemical compound — in 1962 a chemist made xenon tetrafluoride, shocking the scientific world which believed noble gases could never react.
Xenon is used in the super-bright headlights of luxury cars and in the powerful flash lamps used to pump lasers.
NASA uses xenon as the propellant in ion thrusters on spacecraft — electric fields shoot xenon ions out at enormous speed to gently push the craft through space.
Xenon is present in Earth's atmosphere in tiny amounts — only about 90 parts per billion — making it one of the rarest stable gases on our planet.

image_caption: Liquid mercury being poured, showing its extraordinary mirror-like silvery surface.

compounds.name: Cinnabar
compounds.use: The bright red mineral ore of mercury, used as a pigment for thousands of years

compounds.name: Mercury chloride
compounds.use: A powerful disinfectant historically used in medicine, now mostly avoided due to toxicity

compounds.name: Calomel
compounds.use: Used in old medicine and as a reference electrode in chemistry

compounds.name: Mercury oxide
compounds.use: Used in some specialised batteries; its decomposition was used by Lavoisier to discover oxygen

facts.text: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature — you can pour it like water, but it's so dense that a cannonball would float on its surface!
Ancient Chinese emperors drank mercury compounds believing it would grant immortality — it actually poisoned them, possibly contributing to the death of the first emperor Qin Shi Huang.
The phrase 'mad as a hatter' is real — hat-makers in the 1800s used mercury nitrate to treat felt, and the mercury fumes caused brain damage, tremors, and erratic behaviour.
Mercury's chemical symbol Hg comes from its Latin name 'hydrargyrum', meaning 'water silver' — a perfect description of its silvery, flowing appearance.

image_caption: A 140-gram chunk of pure beryllium metal

compounds.name: Beryllium oxide
compounds.use: Used in rocket nozzles and heat shields because it can withstand extreme temperatures

compounds.name: Beryllium sulfate
compounds.use: Used in laboratory research and some X-ray equipment

compounds.name: Beryllium chloride
compounds.use: Used as a catalyst in industrial chemical reactions

facts.text: Beryllium is so light that a golf ball-sized chunk weighs less than a ping-pong ball — it's one of the lightest metals that can handle real heat.
The James Webb Space Telescope's giant golden mirrors are made from beryllium coated in gold, because beryllium stays perfectly stiff even in the freezing cold of space.
Beryllium is dangerously toxic if you breathe in its dust, so scientists have to handle it very carefully with special protective equipment.
Emeralds and aquamarines are both beryllium minerals — the green colour of an emerald comes from chromium atoms sitting inside a beryllium crystal.

image_caption: Sublimed scandium dendrites next to a 1 cm³ reference cube

compounds.name: Scandium oxide
compounds.use: Used to make high-intensity stadium lighting that looks like natural daylight

compounds.name: Scandium chloride
compounds.use: Used in chemical research and as a catalyst

compounds.name: Scandium-aluminium alloy
compounds.use: Used in high-performance baseball bats, bicycle frames, and aerospace parts because it is very strong and light

facts.text: Scandium was predicted to exist by Dmitri Mendeleev before it was discovered — he called it 'eka-boron' and described its properties almost perfectly.
The Soviet Union secretly stockpiled scandium during the Cold War to make ultra-strong aluminium alloys for military aircraft.
Despite being a rare metal, scandium is actually more common in Earth's crust than lead — it's just very spread out and hard to collect.
High-intensity lights in sports stadiums often use scandium iodide, which produces a bright white light that perfectly mimics sunshine.

image_caption: A crystal bar of pure titanium metal

compounds.name: Titanium dioxide
compounds.use: White pigment used in paint, sunscreen, and to make paper brilliantly white

compounds.name: Titanium tetrachloride
compounds.use: Used to make other titanium compounds and as a catalyst in plastic production

compounds.name: Titanium nitride
compounds.use: Extremely hard gold-coloured coating used on drill bits and surgical tools

compounds.name: Titanium carbide
compounds.use: One of the hardest materials known, used in cutting tools and armour

facts.text: Titanium is as strong as steel but 45% lighter, which is why it is used in fighter jets, spacecraft, and racing bicycles.
Your body accepts titanium completely — surgeons use titanium screws, plates, and artificial hip joints because bone grows right onto the metal.
The SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest air-breathing plane ever built, was made mostly from titanium because it got so hot at top speed that aluminium would melt.
Titanium was named after the Titans of Greek mythology — giants of enormous strength — which suits a metal famous for its incredible strength-to-weight ratio.

compounds.name: Vanadium pentoxide
compounds.use: Key component in giant rechargeable flow batteries that store energy from wind and solar farms

compounds.name: Vanadium dioxide

compounds.name: Vanadium trichloride
compounds.use: Used as a catalyst in manufacturing and chemical research

compounds.name: Vanadium trioxide
compounds.use: Used in making special steel alloys

facts.text: Vanadium is named after Vanadis, the Norse goddess of beauty — its many vividly coloured compounds (yellow, orange, blue, green) made it seem poetic to the chemist who discovered it.
Adding a tiny amount of vanadium to steel makes it dramatically stronger — the steel in car chassis, tools, and crankshafts often contains vanadium.
Some sea creatures called sea squirts concentrate vanadium in their blood at levels a million times higher than in the surrounding seawater, though scientists are still figuring out why.
Vanadium flow batteries can store huge amounts of electricity — some are as big as a house and can power a whole neighbourhood.

image_caption: Chromium crystals next to a 1 cm³ reference cube

compounds.name: Chromium oxide
compounds.use: Green pigment used in paints and to give glass a green colour

compounds.name: Chromium trioxide
compounds.use: Used in chrome plating baths to coat metal parts with shiny protective chromium

compounds.name: Potassium dichromate
compounds.use: Used in leather tanning and photography

compounds.name: Chromite
compounds.use: The main ore mineral from which chromium is extracted

facts.text: Chromium's name comes from the Greek word for colour — its compounds appear in almost every colour of the rainbow, from bright red to deep green.
Rubies are red because they contain a tiny amount of chromium — pure aluminium oxide would be colourless, but chromium turns it deep red.
Stainless steel gets its rust-resistant superpower from chromium — adding at least 10.5% chromium causes a thin invisible shield of chromium oxide to form on the surface.
Chrome-plated bumpers and taps get their mirror-bright finish from a thin layer of chromium deposited by passing electricity through a chemical bath.

image_caption: Electrolytic manganese metal next to a 1 cm³ reference cube

compounds.name: Manganese dioxide
compounds.use: The black powder inside ordinary AA batteries that makes them work

compounds.name: Potassium permanganate
compounds.use: A deep purple disinfectant used to treat water and skin infections

compounds.name: Manganese sulfate
compounds.use: Added to fertilisers because plants need tiny amounts of manganese to grow

compounds.name: Manganese tetroxide
compounds.use: Used in making ferrite magnets and in the steel industry

facts.text: Manganese nodules — lumpy black rocks loaded with manganese — litter the deep ocean floor, and there is enough of them to supply the world for thousands of years.
Ancient cave painters used manganese dioxide as a black pigment more than 30,000 years ago — making it one of the oldest materials used by humans as art.
Steel without manganese would be brittle and crack easily — virtually all steel produced today contains a small amount of manganese to keep it tough.
Your brain needs manganese to work properly — it helps make enzymes that protect brain cells from damage, though too much can actually be toxic.

image_caption: Electrolytic cobalt next to a 1 cm³ reference cube

compounds.name: Cobalt oxide
compounds.use: Deep blue colouring used in glass, ceramics, and pottery for thousands of years

compounds.name: Cobalt chloride
compounds.use: Used in weather-indicator cards that turn from blue (dry) to pink (humid)

compounds.name: Lithium cobalt oxide
compounds.use: The material inside the rechargeable battery of almost every smartphone and laptop

compounds.name: Cobalt oxide
compounds.use: Used in rechargeable batteries and as a catalyst for splitting water in solar energy research

facts.text: The word 'cobalt' comes from the German word 'Kobold', meaning goblin — medieval miners blamed mischievous goblins when cobalt ores made them sick while they were trying to smelt silver.
Cobalt is the element inside vitamin B12 — it sits right at the centre of the molecule, making cobalt the only metal that is essential in human vitamins.
The brilliant blue colour in ancient Egyptian glass and Chinese Ming dynasty porcelain both come from cobalt, showing it was valued across cultures for thousands of years.
More than half the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, making it one of the most geographically concentrated critical minerals on Earth.

image_caption: Electrolytic nickel next to a 1 cm³ reference cube

compounds.name: Nickel oxide
compounds.use: Used in ceramics and as a catalyst in chemical production

compounds.name: Nickel chloride
compounds.use: Used in nickel plating baths to coat metal objects with a hard, shiny protective layer

compounds.name: Nickel carbonyl
compounds.use: Highly toxic intermediate used in the Mond process to purify nickel metal

compounds.name: Nickel sulfate
compounds.use: Used in electroplating and in making nickel-based batteries

facts.text: Nickel got its name from the German 'Kupfernickel', meaning 'devil's copper' — miners were fooled by nickel ores that looked like copper but yielded no copper at all.
Earth's core is thought to be made largely of iron and nickel — the same mix found in most metallic meteorites, which are fragments of other planets' cores.
The US five-cent coin is called a 'nickel' but only contains 25% nickel — the rest is copper. Pure nickel coins were used earlier in history.
Nickel is strongly magnetic at room temperature, just like iron and cobalt — it is one of only three elements that are naturally magnetic.

image_caption: A gallium bar cracked open to reveal its crystalline interior

compounds.name: Gallium arsenide
compounds.use: Semiconductor used in solar cells, LED lights, and the chips inside mobile phones

compounds.name: Gallium nitride
compounds.use: Used in blue and white LEDs, Blu-ray disc lasers, and highly efficient phone chargers

compounds.name: Gallium oxide
compounds.use: Next-generation semiconductor material for ultra-efficient power electronics

compounds.name: Gallium chloride
compounds.use: Used in chemical research and as a catalyst

facts.text: Gallium melts at just 29.8°C — it will melt in your hand on a warm day, turning from a silver solid to a shiny liquid right on your palm.
Gallium was one of the elements predicted by Mendeleev before it was discovered — he called it 'eka-aluminium' and guessed its properties almost exactly.
The blue and white LEDs that light up your phone screen and LED light bulbs rely on gallium compounds — the invention earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Gallium expands when it freezes (like water), which is unusual for metals — this means you should never store liquid gallium in a sealed glass container.

image_caption: Polycrystalline germanium showing its distinctive metallic grey lustre

compounds.name: Germanium dioxide
compounds.use: Used to make the glass in fibre-optic cables that carry internet data around the world

compounds.name: Germanium tetrachloride
compounds.use: Key intermediate in making ultra-pure germanium for electronics and fibre optics

compounds.name: Germane
compounds.use: Used in chemical vapour deposition to grow thin semiconductor films

compounds.name: Zinc germanium phosphide
compounds.use: Used in infrared lasers for military and medical imaging

facts.text: Germanium was another element that Mendeleev predicted — he called it 'eka-silicon' in 1871, and when it was discovered in 1886, its properties matched his predictions so closely that it proved his periodic table was right.
The very first transistor ever built, in 1947, was made from germanium — this invention started the entire electronics revolution that gave us computers and smartphones.
Germanium is transparent to infrared light, even though it looks like a shiny grey metal — this makes it perfect for night-vision goggles and thermal cameras.
Named after Germany (Germania in Latin), germanium was discovered by German chemist Clemens Winkler in 1886.

image_caption: A sample of grey metallic arsenic

compounds.name: Arsenic trioxide
compounds.use: Used in very small, carefully controlled doses to treat a specific type of leukaemia

compounds.name: Gallium arsenide
compounds.use: Semiconductor used in solar cells and the chips inside mobile phones

compounds.name: Arsenic trisulfide
compounds.use: Used as a yellow pigment (orpiment) in ancient art and as an infrared optical material

compounds.name: Calcium arsenite
compounds.use: Formerly used as a pesticide, now mostly banned due to toxicity

facts.text: Arsenic was the poison of choice for murderers throughout history and was nicknamed 'inheritance powder' in Renaissance Italy because it helped heirs speed up their inheritance — it was nearly undetectable until the 1830s.
Napoleon Bonaparte may have been slowly poisoned by arsenic from the green wallpaper in his damp St Helena bedroom — the damp caused mould to convert arsenic-based dye into toxic gas.
Despite its deadly reputation, arsenic compounds are used today as targeted cancer treatments — arsenic trioxide can put a certain type of leukaemia into remission.
Arsenic occurs naturally in groundwater in parts of Bangladesh and West Bengal, affecting millions of people — it is one of the world's largest environmental health crises.

image_caption: Distilled strontium crystals with a freshly cut, shiny surface

compounds.name: Strontium carbonate
compounds.use: The red colour in fireworks and emergency flares — strontium burns with a brilliant crimson flame

compounds.name: Strontium sulfate
compounds.use: The main mineral ore of strontium (celestite); also used in drilling fluids for oil wells

compounds.name: Strontium chloride
compounds.use: Used in toothpaste for sensitive teeth to reduce pain

compounds.name: Strontium titanate
compounds.use: Synthetic diamond simulant with even more sparkle than real diamond

facts.text: Strontium gives fireworks and flares their vivid red colour — every bright crimson burst you see in a firework display contains a strontium compound.
Strontium-90, a radioactive isotope produced in nuclear explosions, was a major health concern during Cold War nuclear testing because the body mistakes it for calcium and stores it in bones.
Strontium was named after Strontian, a small village in Scotland, where the mineral strontianite was first discovered in a lead mine in 1790.
Strontium titanate can be cut into gemstones that sparkle more brilliantly than diamonds, though it is softer and scratches more easily.

image_caption: Barium metal stored under argon gas to prevent it reacting with air

compounds.name: Barium sulfate
compounds.use: Drunk as a 'barium meal' before X-rays of the gut — it is opaque to X-rays and shows the shape of the digestive tract

compounds.name: Barium carbonate
compounds.use: Used in making specialty glass, ceramics, and rat poison

compounds.name: Barium oxide
compounds.use: Used in cathode ray tube glass and as a drying agent in laboratories

compounds.name: Barium chloride
compounds.use: Used in water treatment, fireworks (green colour), and making other barium compounds

facts.text: Barium's name comes from the Greek 'barys', meaning heavy — barium sulfate is so dense that doctors use it to make the inside of your stomach visible on an X-ray.
Barium burns with a vivid green flame — you can spot it in fireworks displays as the bright apple-green bursts.
Pure barium metal is so reactive it catches fire spontaneously in air and reacts violently with water, so it must always be stored under oil or inert gas.
Barium is used in vacuum tubes — getters made of barium absorb the last traces of gas inside the tube, keeping the vacuum perfect.

compounds.name: Tungsten trioxide

compounds.name: Tungsten carbide
compounds.use: Extremely hard material used in drill bits, cutting tools, and the tips of ball-point pens

compounds.name: Tungsten disulfide
compounds.use: Dry lubricant used in spacecraft and high-temperature machinery

compounds.name: Sodium tungstate
compounds.use: Used as a flame retardant and in making tungsten-based pigments

facts.text: Tungsten's chemical symbol is W because its German name is Wolfram — German scientists discovered it first, and Wolfram is still the official name in many European languages.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal — 3,422°C — which is why old-fashioned light bulb filaments were made from it; it glows white-hot without melting.
A golf club driver with a tiny tungsten weight in just the right place can add metres to your drive — engineers use its extreme density to fine-tune the balance of sports equipment.
Tungsten is so dense that a cube the size of a tennis ball would weigh about 4 kg — nearly as heavy as a bag of sugar.

compounds.name: Cisplatin

compounds.name: Platinum oxide
compounds.use: Catalyst used in hydrogenation reactions in the pharmaceutical and food industries

facts.text: Platinum is rarer than gold — all the platinum ever mined in history would fit inside your living room, forming a cube about 8 metres on each side.
The catalytic converter in a car's exhaust pipe contains platinum — it triggers reactions that turn poisonous gases like carbon monoxide into harmless carbon dioxide and water.
From 1889 to 2019, the official definition of one kilogram was based on a platinum-iridium cylinder kept in a vault near Paris — the world's unit of mass was literally a platinum object.
Platinum is so chemically unreactive that it can be worn as jewellery for decades without tarnishing — even strong acids leave it completely untouched.

image_caption: A sample of radium-226 metal, which glows faintly blue due to its radioactivity

compounds.name: Radium chloride
compounds.use: The compound Marie Curie first isolated to identify radium; historically used in cancer radiation therapy

compounds.name: Radium bromide
compounds.use: Used in early radiation therapy and scientific research in the early 1900s

compounds.name: Radium sulfate
compounds.use: Extremely insoluble salt used in early studies of radioactivity

facts.text: Marie Curie discovered radium in 1898, working in a leaky shed in Paris — she processed tonnes of pitchblende ore by hand, not knowing the radiation was slowly making her fatally ill.
Radium glows blue in the dark because its radiation excites the air molecules around it — early 20th-century watch dials were painted with radium so soldiers could read them at night.

The 'Radium Girls' were factory workers in the 1920s who painted watch dials with radium paint and were told to lick their brushes to a fine point — many died of radiation poisoning, and their case changed workplace safety laws forever.
Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes — one in Physics and one in Chemistry — making her the first person ever to win in two different sciences, and she remains the only woman to have done so.

compounds.name: Uranium dioxide

compounds.name: Uranium hexafluoride

compounds.name: Triuranium octoxide
compounds.use: Yellowcake — the concentrated uranium ore powder shipped from uranium mines

compounds.name: Uranyl nitrate
compounds.use: Used in nuclear fuel reprocessing and as a stain in electron microscopy

facts.text: Uranium was named after the planet Uranus, which had just been discovered eight years earlier — it was the first element to be named after a planet.

A single uranium fuel pellet the size of your thumb contains as much energy as 17,000 cubic feet of natural gas, 1,780 pounds of coal, or 149 gallons of oil — making nuclear power incredibly energy-dense.

Uranium was used as an orange-yellow glass colourant for over a century before anyone knew it was radioactive — antique 'Vaseline glass' glows green under ultraviolet light because of its uranium content.

Uranium is actually one of the most common heavy elements in Earth's crust — it is more abundant than silver, and the heat it produces as it slowly decays is one reason the inside of the Earth stays hot.

facts.text: Selenium is an essential nutrient — your body needs tiny amounts of it to make antioxidant proteins that protect your cells from damage.
Selenium conducts electricity much better in bright light than in the dark, so early photocopiers and solar cells used it to detect light.
Brazil nuts are by far the richest food source of selenium — just two nuts can give you your entire recommended daily amount.
Selenium was discovered in 1817 and named after Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, because it was found alongside the element tellurium, named for the Earth.

facts.text: Rubidium is so reactive that it bursts into a purplish-red flame the instant it touches air — it must be stored sealed in dry mineral oil or argon gas.
Rubidium atomic clocks are used in GPS satellites to keep time accurate to a billionth of a second, helping your phone's maps pinpoint your exact location.
Rubidium melts at just 39°C — barely above room temperature — so a nugget of it would melt in a warm room on a summer's day.
It was discovered in 1861 using a brand-new technique called spectroscopy, where scientists identify elements by the unique colours their flames produce.

facts.text: Yttrium is named after Ytterby, a small village in Sweden — the quarry there was so packed with rare minerals that four elements were eventually named after it.
The bright red phosphor in old colour television sets was made from yttrium oxide — without it, TVs could not display vivid reds.
Yttrium is used to make YAG lasers that surgeons use to zap kidney stones and remove tumours without cutting a single stitch.
It is classed as a rare earth metal even though it is actually more abundant in the Earth's crust than lead.

facts.text: Cubic zirconia — a man-made form of zirconium dioxide — is one of the most popular diamond substitutes in jewellery because it sparkles almost as brilliantly but costs a fraction of the price.
Zirconium is used to coat the fuel rods inside nuclear reactors because it barely absorbs neutrons, letting the chain reaction keep going.
Zircon crystals are the oldest objects ever found on Earth — some have been dated to 4.4 billion years old, only 100 million years after the planet formed.
Zirconium metal burns with a brilliant white flame and is used in military flares and fireworks to create dazzling white sparks.

facts.text: Niobium is named after Niobe from Greek mythology, daughter of Tantalus — it was named this way because niobium was always found alongside tantalum in nature.
Adding a tiny amount of niobium to steel makes it dramatically stronger — most of the steel used in car bodies and pipelines today contains niobium.
Niobium becomes a superconductor at very low temperatures, carrying electricity with zero resistance, and is used in the powerful magnets inside MRI scanners.
Brazil produces about 90% of the world's niobium — a single mine there supplies most of the steel industry's needs worldwide.

facts.text: Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of any element at 2,623°C — making it vital for jet engine parts and rocket nozzles that must survive extreme heat.
All living things need molybdenum in tiny amounts — it sits at the active centre of enzymes that help bacteria fix nitrogen from the air into soil.
Molybdenum disulfide is a brilliant solid lubricant — slipperier than graphite — and is used to lubricate machinery in space where liquid oils would evaporate.
It was named from the Greek word for lead ('molybdos') because its main ore, molybdenite, was often confused with graphite and lead ore by early miners.

compounds.name: Technetium heptoxide
compounds.use: Intermediate used in preparing technetium compounds for research

facts.text: Technetium was the very first element to be made artificially — it does not exist naturally on Earth because all its atoms are radioactive and have long since decayed away.
It was created in 1937 by bombarding molybdenum with neutrons in a particle accelerator — scientists had predicted a gap in the periodic table where it should be, and they finally filled it.

Despite being radioactive, a form of technetium called Tc-99m is used in millions of medical scans every year — injected into patients, it travels to specific organs and emits gamma rays that cameras can detect.
Technetium is so rare that the total amount ever produced in laboratories worldwide would barely fill a teaspoon.

compounds.name: Ruthenium dioxide
compounds.use: Coating on electrodes used to produce chlorine gas industrially

compounds.name: Ruthenium tetroxide
compounds.use: Used in chemistry labs to oxidise organic compounds

compounds.name: Ruthenium bipyridyl
compounds.use: Key dye used in early prototype solar cells

facts.text: Ruthenium is named after Ruthenia, the Latin name for Russia, as it was discovered in ores from the Ural Mountains in 1844.
Adding just a trace of ruthenium to titanium or platinum makes those metals dramatically harder and more resistant to wear — a gram of ruthenium can toughen kilograms of other metal.
Ruthenium is one of the rarest elements on Earth, found mainly as a by-product when processing nickel and copper ores, making it precious and expensive.
Hard disk drives in computers use a thin ruthenium layer to increase the density of magnetic storage, allowing more data to fit on a smaller disk.

compounds.name: Rhodium chloride

compounds.name: Rhodium oxide
compounds.use: Used in some high-temperature catalytic applications

facts.text: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive metals on Earth — at times it has cost more than ten times the price of gold.
The catalytic converter in a car's exhaust system contains a tiny amount of rhodium that converts poisonous carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into harmless gases.
Rhodium is so shiny and resistant to tarnish that jewellery and silverware are often given a thin rhodium plating to keep them bright and scratch-free.
It was discovered in 1803 and named after the Greek word for rose ('rhodon') because some of its dissolved compounds are a striking rose-red colour.

compounds.name: Palladium chloride
compounds.use: Used as a catalyst in organic chemistry and in tests for carbon monoxide leaks

compounds.name: Palladium acetate
compounds.use: Catalyst used to build complex carbon molecules in pharmaceuticals

facts.text: Palladium can absorb up to 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas — scientists are exploring this remarkable property for storing hydrogen fuel in clean-energy vehicles.
Like rhodium, palladium is a key metal inside catalytic converters, helping to break down harmful pollutants in car exhaust into less harmful gases.
Palladium is named after the asteroid Pallas, which was discovered just before the metal in 1803 — its discoverer William Wollaston loved the connection between science and astronomy.
Palladium is used in dentistry as an alloy for crowns and bridges because it is strong, non-toxic, and does not corrode inside the mouth.

compounds.name: Cadmium sulfide

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride

compounds.name: Cadmium selenide

facts.text: Cadmium is extremely toxic — it accumulates in the body over a lifetime and can cause kidney failure and a painful bone disease called Itai-itai ('ouch-ouch') disease, first seen in Japan.
The vivid yellow and orange pigments made from cadmium sulfide were beloved by 20th-century artists, including Henri Matisse, for their brilliant, stable colours.
Cadmium-telluride solar panels are now one of the cheapest types of solar technology, helping to bring down the cost of renewable electricity worldwide.
Cadmium was discovered in 1817 as an impurity in zinc carbonate — it is nearly always found alongside zinc in nature, since their atoms are very similar in size.

image_caption: A pure indium metal sample

compounds.name: Indium oxide

compounds.name: Indium phosphide
compounds.use: Used in high-speed electronics and fibre-optic laser diodes

compounds.name: Indium arsenide
compounds.use: Used in infrared detectors and night-vision cameras

facts.text: Indium tin oxide (ITO) is the invisible conducting film on every smartphone, tablet, and touchscreen — without indium, modern touchscreens would not work.
Indium is so soft you can scratch it with a fingernail, and when you bend a rod of pure indium it makes a distinctive crackling sound called a 'tin cry'.
It was discovered in 1863 and named after the deep indigo-blue colour it produces in a flame — one of the most beautiful colours in spectroscopy at the time.
Indium is mainly extracted as a by-product of zinc smelting; the entire world's annual production would fit inside a modest garden shed.

image_caption: Antimony metal showing its characteristic lustre

compounds.name: Antimony trioxide
compounds.use: Flame retardant added to plastics, textiles, and electronics

compounds.name: Antimony sulfide

compounds.name: Antimony chloride
compounds.use: Used as a mordant in dyeing fabrics and in some laboratory processes

facts.text: Ancient Egyptians used black antimony sulfide as kohl eyeliner — archaeologists have found antimony-based cosmetics in tombs over 5,000 years old.
Antimony trioxide is one of the most widely used flame retardants in the world — it is blended into plastics to make electronic gadgets and furniture less likely to catch fire.
Type metal — used to cast the movable type that printed books for centuries — was an alloy of lead and antimony, because antimony expands slightly on cooling and makes crisp, sharp letters.

Its symbol Sb comes from its Latin name 'stibium', which has been used since ancient times, while the English name 'antimony' may derive from Greek words meaning 'not alone' — it is rarely found pure in nature.

image_caption: Crystalline tellurium showing its metallic lustre

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride
compounds.use: Used in thin-film solar panels

compounds.name: Bismuth telluride
