compounds.name: Hydrogen telluride
compounds.use: An extremely foul-smelling gas used in some semiconductor research

facts.text: Tellurium is named after Tellus, the Latin name for Earth — it was the partner element to selenium, which is named after the Moon.
Pure tellurium has a garlic-like smell, and people who handle it absorb trace amounts through their skin that can make their breath smell strongly of garlic for weeks.
Bismuth telluride is a thermoelectric material that can turn a temperature difference directly into electricity — small devices using it power remote scientific sensors without any moving parts.
Tellurium is one of the rarest stable elements on Earth — it is actually rarer in the Earth's crust than platinum, which is why it is classified as a critical mineral.

image_caption: Caesium metal sealed in a glass ampoule — it glows pale gold

compounds.name: Caesium chloride
compounds.use: Used in lab centrifuges to separate DNA by density

compounds.name: Caesium hydroxide
compounds.use: One of the strongest known alkali bases

compounds.name: Caesium carbonate
compounds.use: Used in organic chemistry reactions as a mild base

facts.text: Caesium atomic clocks are the world's most precise timekeepers — the international definition of one second is based on exactly 9,192,631,770 vibrations of caesium-133 atoms.
GPS satellites, the internet, and global financial systems all depend on caesium atomic clocks to stay synchronised to within a few nanoseconds per day.
Caesium is one of only two metals that are liquid at room temperature on a warm day — it melts at 28.5°C, just above typical room temperature.
When caesium touches water it explodes with an impressive violet flash — it reacts far more violently than sodium or potassium.

image_caption: A sample of lanthanum metal

compounds.name: Lanthanum oxide
compounds.use: Added to special optical glass lenses to reduce light scattering

compounds.name: Lanthanum nickel alloy
compounds.use: Used in nickel-metal hydride rechargeable batteries

compounds.name: Lanthanum chloride
compounds.use: Used in research and as a phosphor activator

facts.text: The rechargeable nickel-metal hydride battery in early hybrid cars like the Toyota Prius contained several kilograms of lanthanum — your family car may have run partly on rare earth metals.
Lanthanum is one of the most common rare earth elements — despite the name 'rare earth', it is more abundant in the Earth's crust than lead.
Adding lanthanum to glass greatly improves its optical quality, allowing camera and microscope lenses to focus light more precisely without distorting colours.
It was named from the Greek word 'lanthanein', meaning 'to lie hidden', because it hid undetected inside cerium oxide for decades before being isolated in 1839.

image_caption: A sample of cerium metal

compounds.name: Cerium dioxide
compounds.use: Used to polish glass, computer chips, and gemstones; also in catalytic converters

compounds.name: Cerium oxide
compounds.use: Used in self-cleaning oven coatings

compounds.name: Cerium chloride
compounds.use: Used as a catalyst in organic chemistry reactions

facts.text: Cerium is the most abundant rare earth element — it is more common in the Earth's crust than copper, and it is the rare earth used most heavily by industry.
The flint in disposable cigarette lighters and camping firestarters is actually an alloy called 'mischmetal' that is 50% cerium — it produces sparks when scratched.
Cerium dioxide is used to polish the glass of smartphones, camera lenses, and silicon computer chips to an almost perfect mirror flatness measured in nanometres.
Cerium was discovered in 1803 and named after the dwarf planet Ceres, which had been discovered only two years earlier — naming elements after astronomical objects was fashionable at the time.

image_caption: A hafnium crystal bar

compounds.name: Hafnium dioxide
compounds.use: Used as insulating layer in modern computer microchips

compounds.name: Hafnium carbide
compounds.use: Has one of the highest melting points of any compound — used in extreme heat applications

compounds.name: Hafnium chloride
compounds.use: Used to deposit hafnium films in microchip manufacturing

facts.text: Hafnium was the last stable element to be discovered — in 1923, hidden in zirconium ore that chemists had been using for over a century without realising a second element was lurking inside.
Hafnium absorbs neutrons extremely well, making it the ideal control rod material in nuclear reactors — sliding hafnium rods into a reactor core slows or stops the chain reaction.
Modern Intel and AMD computer chips use hafnium dioxide as a key insulating layer — without it, transistors could not shrink further and smartphones would still be the size of bricks.
Hafnium was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen — it was discovered there by scientists Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy.

image_caption: Tantalum single crystal and a 1 cm³ cube

compounds.name: Tantalum pentoxide
compounds.use: Used as a capacitor material in mobile phones and laptops

compounds.name: Tantalum carbide
compounds.use: Used in cutting tool tips that must withstand extreme heat

compounds.name: Tantalum chloride
compounds.use: Used in chemical vapour deposition to make thin tantalum films

facts.text: Tantalum capacitors are inside virtually every smartphone and laptop — a tiny amount of tantalum stores and releases electrical charge rapidly, helping electronics run smoothly.
Tantalum is almost completely inert inside the human body and does not corrode, making it ideal for surgical implants such as skull plates, hip joints, and jaw reconstruction.
The mineral coltan, found mainly in the Democratic Republic of Congo, contains tantalum — demand for smartphones has made it a valuable and at times conflict-fuelling resource.

It is named after Tantalus from Greek mythology, who was condemned to stand in a pool of water under fruit trees that retreated whenever he reached for them — tantalum was notoriously difficult to isolate from its ore.

image_caption: Rhenium single crystal bar and a 1 cm³ cube

compounds.name: Rhenium heptoxide
compounds.use: Used as a catalyst in the production of high-octane fuels

compounds.name: Rhenium trioxide
compounds.use: One of the few non-metallic compounds that conducts electricity like a metal

facts.text: Rhenium has one of the highest melting points of all elements at 3,186°C — only tungsten melts at a higher temperature — making it indispensable in jet and rocket engines.
Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered — in 1925, making it the final non-radioactive element to be found in nature.
Nickel superalloy blades inside modern jet turbines contain around 6% rhenium — this allows the blades to survive the searing 1,400°C gas temperatures inside a running engine.
Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust — it is mostly recovered as a by-product of roasting molybdenum ores, and the whole world produces only about 50 tonnes a year.

image_caption: Crystalline osmium with its characteristic blue-white lustre

compounds.name: Osmium tetroxide
compounds.use: Used in electron microscopy to stain biological samples; extremely toxic

compounds.name: Osmium dioxide
compounds.use: Used in some catalytic and research applications

facts.text: Osmium is the densest element on Earth — a cube of osmium the size of a tennis ball would weigh about 4 kg, nearly twice as heavy as the same sized cube of lead.
Osmium tetroxide has an unmistakable sharp smell — the name osmium comes from the Greek word 'osme' meaning 'smell', and even tiny amounts are detectable by nose.
Before tungsten took over, osmium was mixed with iridium to make the tips of fountain pen nibs — osmium-iridium alloy is extraordinarily hard and resists the wear of millions of writing strokes.

Osmium tetroxide is used in electron microscopy to stain the fatty membranes of cells so they show up clearly — it is one of the most powerful staining agents in biology, but also one of the most toxic.

image_caption: Pieces of pure iridium metal

compounds.name: Iridium dioxide
compounds.use: Used in electrodes for water splitting to produce hydrogen fuel

compounds.name: Iridium chloride
compounds.use: Starting material for making iridium catalysts and coatings

facts.text: A thin layer of iridium-rich clay was found worldwide at the geological boundary 66 million years ago — evidence that a giant asteroid (which also contains high levels of iridium) wiped out the dinosaurs.
Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant element known — it barely reacts with any acid, even aqua regia (the mix that dissolves gold), and stays shiny for millions of years.
The international kilogram standard — the platinum cylinder kept in Paris that all scales worldwide were once calibrated against — contained 10% iridium to make it harder and more durable.
Iridium is named after Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its dissolved salts form a striking range of brilliantly coloured compounds.

image_caption: Thallium metal pieces in a sealed glass ampoule

compounds.name: Thallium sulfate
compounds.use: Once used as a rodent and ant poison — now banned in most countries

compounds.name: Thallium bromide
compounds.use: Used in infrared detectors and radiation sensors

compounds.name: Thallium oxide
compounds.use: Used to make high-refractive-index glass for specialised lenses

facts.text: Thallium is extremely poisonous — it is odourless, tasteless, and colourless in solution, and for decades thallium sulfate was used as a secret murder weapon, earning it the nickname 'inheritance powder'.
Thallium poisoning causes hair to fall out — this was once used as a medical treatment for ringworm of the scalp before safer drugs were found, which seems unbelievably harsh today.

Thallium was discovered in 1861 by William Crookes using spectroscopy — he noticed a vivid green spectral line he had never seen before and named the element after the Greek word for a green shoot ('thallos').

Despite its toxicity, thallium has a useful role in medicine — radioactive thallium-201 is injected into patients during cardiac stress tests to show how well blood is flowing through the heart muscle.

image_caption: Bismuth crystals showing rainbow oxide colours, and a 1 cm³ cube

compounds.name: Bismuth oxide
compounds.use: Used in pigments, cosmetics, and as a catalyst

compounds.name: Bismuth iodide
compounds.use: Investigated as a non-toxic semiconductor for solar cells

compounds.name: Bismuth subsalicylate
compounds.use: Active ingredient in stomach medicines like Pepto-Bismol

facts.text: Bismuth is one of the safest heavy metals — it is used in medicines like Pepto-Bismol to soothe upset stomachs, and as a non-toxic replacement for lead in shotgun pellets and fishing weights.
When bismuth cools slowly after melting, it forms spectacular staircase-shaped crystals with rainbow-coloured surfaces caused by an ultra-thin layer of iridescent oxide.
Bismuth expands very slightly when it solidifies, unlike most metals which shrink — this makes it useful in alloys for castings that need to fill a mould perfectly, such as sprinkler heads.
Bismuth-209 was long thought to be the heaviest stable element, but in 2003 scientists proved it is actually very slightly radioactive — its half-life is a billion times older than the universe.

image_caption: A sample of polonium on a brass sheet

facts.text: Polonium was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie, and Marie named it after Poland — her homeland, which at the time was not recognised as an independent country.
Polonium is incredibly radioactive — just one gram emits as much radiation as 4,500 kg of radium and glows with a faint blue light from the air it ionises around it.
Marie Curie won two Nobel prizes — for Physics (1903, shared with Pierre) and for Chemistry (1911) — becoming the first person ever to win in two different sciences.

In 2006, former Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko was murdered with a tiny amount of polonium-210 slipped into his tea in London — it remains one of history's most dramatic uses of a radioactive element as a weapon.

image_caption: Glow from a microscopic sample of astatine

facts.text: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth — the entire planet contains only about 28 grams of astatine at any one time, all of it constantly decaying and being replaced.
The most stable form of astatine has a half-life of just 8.1 hours, meaning half of it disappears every eight hours — you could never see it with the naked eye because it decays far too fast.
Despite being so rare and radioactive, astatine is promising in cancer treatment — astatine-211 can be attached to molecules that seek out tumour cells and destroy them from the inside.
Its name comes from the Greek word 'astatos' meaning unstable — a fitting name for an element that barely exists long enough to study.

image_caption: Emission spectrum of radon-222 gas

facts.text: Radon is a colourless, odourless, radioactive gas that seeps up from uranium-containing rocks in the ground — it can accumulate in the basements of houses and is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
Radon is produced naturally as uranium and thorium decay underground, and it seeps up through cracks in soil and building foundations — areas built on granite rock often have higher radon levels.

In many countries, homes are tested for radon and fitted with simple ventilation systems to draw the gas away before it builds up to dangerous levels — a straightforward fix that saves thousands of lives.

Radon was discovered in 1900 as a mysterious emanation from radium — Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy realised that radioactive elements spontaneously transform into other elements, a revolutionary idea at the time.
Francium is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth — at any moment, the entire planet contains an estimated 20 to 30 grams of it, scattered in trace amounts across uranium ore deposits.

It was discovered in 1939 by French physicist Marguerite Perey, who named it after France — she was the last person to discover a naturally occurring element, and the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences.
The most stable isotope of francium has a half-life of just 22 minutes — it decays into radium or astatine so quickly that bulk francium metal has never been seen by any scientist.
Because francium sits directly below caesium in the periodic table, it should be even more violently reactive with water than caesium — but no one has ever had enough of it at once to find out.

image_caption: Actinium sample glowing blue from its own radioactivity

facts.text: Actinium glows with an eerie blue light in the dark, caused by the radioactive particles it fires off ionising the surrounding air — scientists can see it glowing when they work with it in a dark room.
Actinium gave its name to the 'actinides' — the bottom row of the periodic table containing all the heaviest elements from actinium to lawrencium.
Actinium-225 is one of the most promising materials in cancer medicine — it emits very short-range alpha radiation that can destroy tumour cells while causing minimal damage to healthy tissue.
It was discovered in 1899 by André-Louis Debierne, a close colleague of Marie Curie, just one year after she announced the discovery of polonium and radium.

image_caption: A 0.1 g sample of thorium metal in a glass ampoule

compounds.name: Thorium dioxide
compounds.use: Used to make gas mantles for camping lanterns — they glow brilliantly white when heated

compounds.name: Thorium nitrate
compounds.use: Used in some optical glass formulations

facts.text: Thorium is a promising nuclear fuel — a tonne of thorium can produce as much energy as 200 tonnes of uranium or 3.5 million tonnes of coal, with much less long-lived radioactive waste.
The white glow of old-fashioned camping lanterns (the fabric sock part called a mantle) came from thorium oxide — when heated by a gas flame, it produced a brilliantly bright white light.
India has some of the world's largest thorium deposits and is actively developing thorium-fuelled nuclear reactors, hoping to power the country for centuries on domestic fuel.
Thorium was named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder — it was discovered in 1829 by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who also discovered several other elements.

image_caption: A small sample of protactinium-231 in a glass vial

facts.text: Protactinium means 'before actinium' — when it decays it turns into actinium, so it is literally the element that comes before actinium in a radioactive decay chain.
Protactinium-231 has a half-life of 32,760 years, meaning it accumulates slowly in uranium ores over geological time and can be extracted in tiny amounts.
Scientists use the ratio of protactinium-231 to thorium-230 in ocean sediment cores as a geological clock, measuring ocean circulation patterns thousands of years into the past.
Isolating the first significant sample — just 125 grams — required processing 60 tonnes of uranium ore, making it one of the most laborious element preparations in history.

image_caption: A sample of neptunium-237 in a glass vial

facts.text: Neptunium was the first transuranium element ever made — in 1940, scientists at Berkeley bombarded uranium with neutrons and created something that had never existed before: an element heavier than uranium.
It is named after the planet Neptune, continuing the pattern set by uranium (Uranus) — each heavier element was named after the next planet out in the solar system.
Neptunium-237 is produced in small quantities inside every nuclear reactor, building up gradually as uranium absorbs neutrons.

Despite being man-made, neptunium-239 actually exists in vanishingly tiny amounts in uranium ore, formed when uranium atoms occasionally absorb neutrons from natural radioactive decay — making it technically a natural element.

image_caption: A ring of plutonium metal shaped to prevent nuclear criticality

facts.text: Space probes like Voyager 1 and 2, New Horizons (which flew past Pluto), and the Mars Curiosity rover are powered by plutonium — they use the heat from its radioactive decay to generate electricity billions of kilometres from the Sun.
Plutonium-239 can sustain a nuclear chain reaction — the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in 1945 used about 6 kg of plutonium, releasing energy equivalent to 21,000 tonnes of TNT.
Plutonium is an extremely strange metal — it exists in six different crystal structures at ordinary pressures, and it actually shrinks when it melts, the opposite of almost every other element.
Named after Pluto (then still called a planet), plutonium was the third element in a row named after outer planets — uranium (Uranus), neptunium (Neptune), plutonium (Pluto).

image_caption: A small disc of americium-241 metal viewed under a microscope

compounds.name: Americium dioxide
compounds.use: The form of americium sealed inside household smoke detectors

facts.text: There is a tiny amount of americium-241 inside almost every ionisation smoke detector in your home — it emits a small stream of particles that ionise the air, creating a tiny electrical current; smoke breaks that current and triggers the alarm.
Each smoke detector contains only about 0.3 micrograms of americium — so little that you could fit the americium from thousands of detectors onto a pinhead, yet it is enough to detect a house fire.

Americium was first made in 1944 during the Manhattan Project and named after the Americas — its discoverer Glenn Seaborg actually revealed its existence on a US radio quiz show for children before officially publishing the finding.
Americium is the only synthetic element that most people interact with regularly — every time you test your smoke alarm, you are in a very small way handling nuclear technology.

image_caption: A piece of curium metal in a quartz tube

facts.text: Curium was named after Marie and Pierre Curie in honour of their pioneering research on radioactivity — it is one of the few elements named after a couple rather than a single scientist.
The Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity carried a curium-244 source as part of an alpha particle X-ray spectrometer (APXS) that analysed the chemical composition of Martian rocks and soil.
Curium glows with a faint reddish light in the dark — not because of any chemical reaction, but because its intense radioactivity heats the metal itself, making it thermally luminescent.

Like americium, curium was first made at the University of Chicago Metallurgical Laboratory in 1944, but its discovery was kept classified for two years because of wartime secrecy around nuclear research.

image_caption: Praseodymium metal — a soft, silvery-white rare earth element

compounds.name: Praseodymium oxide
compounds.use: Gives glass and ceramics a vivid yellow-green colour

compounds.name: Praseodymium fluoride
compounds.use: Used in carbon arc lights for film studios and searchlights

facts.text: Praseodymium's name comes from Greek for 'leek-green twin' — its salts produce a distinctive green colour.
Praseodymium is used in high-powered magnets combined with neodymium, making motors in electric vehicles.
Welder's and glassblower's goggles often contain praseodymium to filter out harmful yellow sodium glare.
It was discovered in 1885 when a chemist split a substance thought to be a single element into two — praseodymium and neodymium.

image_caption: A piece of neodymium metal — shiny when freshly cut but tarnishes quickly in air

compounds.name: Neodymium magnet alloy
compounds.use: Strongest permanent magnets ever made — used in headphones, hard drives, and electric motors

compounds.name: Neodymium-doped YAG crystal
compounds.use: Powers the lasers used in laser pointers, eye surgery, and metal cutting

compounds.name: Neodymium oxide
compounds.use: Gives glass a striking violet-purple colour

facts.text: A neodymium magnet the size of a golf ball is strong enough to snap your fingers if you're not careful — they are by far the most powerful permanent magnets in the world.
Almost every electric car, wind turbine, and hard drive relies on neodymium magnets.
The name 'neodymium' means 'new twin' — it was separated from praseodymium in 1885.
Neodymium-doped glass filters out the yellow glare in glassblowers' safety glasses so they can see clearly while working.

compounds.name: Promethium chloride
compounds.use: Used in research; no commercial applications due to radioactivity

facts.text: Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes — every atom eventually decays, so there is almost none left in Earth's crust.
It is produced in nuclear reactors as a by-product of uranium splitting, which is the main source of the tiny amounts we use.
In the 1960s, promethium was used in luminous watch dials and tiny atomic batteries in pacemakers and satellites.
Promethium is named after Prometheus, the Greek Titan who stole fire from the gods — fitting for a radioactive element born in nuclear reactors.

image_caption: Samarium metal — a bright silvery rare earth element

compounds.name: Samarium-cobalt magnet
compounds.use: High-temperature permanent magnets used in jet engines and high-end headphones

compounds.name: Samarium oxide
compounds.use: Used as a neutron absorber in nuclear reactor control rods

facts.text: Samarium-cobalt magnets were the strongest magnets in the world before neodymium magnets appeared — and they still win at high temperatures where neodymium fails.
Samarium is named after the mineral samarskite, which was itself named after a Russian mining official named Samarski.
Samarium-153 is a radioactive isotope used in medicine to relieve bone pain caused by cancer spreading to the skeleton.
Samarium absorbs neutrons so well that it is used in nuclear reactors to help control the chain reaction safely.

image_caption: Europium metal — it oxidises so quickly it must be stored under oil

compounds.name: Europium oxide
compounds.use: Produces the bright red colour in TV and computer screens

compounds.name: Europium hexaboride
compounds.use: Used in specialised electron emitters

facts.text: The red and blue pixels in old CRT televisions glowed because of europium compounds — without it, screens would look dull and yellowish.
Euro banknotes contain europium compounds that glow a distinctive red and blue under ultraviolet light, making them extremely hard to counterfeit.
Europium is the most reactive of all the rare earth metals — it tarnishes in seconds and reacts with water just like sodium does.
Europium was named after Europe in 1901, making it one of the few elements named after an entire continent.

image_caption: Gadolinium metal — a shiny, malleable silvery-white element

compounds.name: Gadolinium chelate (contrast agent)
compounds.use: Injected before MRI scans to make soft tissue and blood vessels visible

compounds.name: Gadolinium oxide
compounds.use: Used in neutron radiography and X-ray screens

compounds.name: Gadolinium iron garnet
compounds.use: Used in microwave components and data storage research

facts.text: When you have an MRI scan with contrast dye, you are most likely being injected with a gadolinium compound — it makes soft tissues show up clearly on the scan.
Gadolinium absorbs more neutrons per atom than almost any other element, making it valuable in nuclear reactor shielding.
At room temperature, gadolinium is magnetic — one of only four elements (along with iron, nickel, and cobalt) that behave this way.
It is named after Johan Gadolin, the Finnish chemist who discovered the first rare earth element back in 1794.

image_caption: Terbium metal — a soft, silvery-grey rare earth element

compounds.name: Terbium oxide
compounds.use: Produces bright green phosphorescence in energy-saving light bulbs and TV screens

compounds.name: Terfenol-D alloy
compounds.use: Changes shape in a magnetic field — used in sonar and precision actuators

facts.text: Terbium produces the green colour in fluorescent lamps and LED phosphors — that crisp white light from energy-saving bulbs partly comes from terbium.
A terbium alloy called Terfenol-D changes its shape when placed in a magnetic field, a property used in sonar systems on submarines.
Terbium is one of four elements (along with yttrium, erbium, and ytterbium) all named after the same village — Ytterby, Sweden, where a remarkable mineral was found.
Terbium is so rare that global production amounts to only a few hundred tonnes per year, nearly all from China.

image_caption: Dysprosium metal chips — a soft, silvery rare earth element

compounds.name: Dysprosium oxide
compounds.use: Added to neodymium magnets to make them withstand higher temperatures in electric vehicle motors

compounds.name: Dysprosium iodide
compounds.use: Used in high-intensity metal halide lamps

facts.text: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek word 'dysprositos', meaning 'hard to get' — it took years of painstaking chemistry to isolate it.
Adding a tiny amount of dysprosium to neodymium magnets stops them from losing their magnetism in hot electric motor environments.
Dysprosium has the highest magnetic strength of any element, which is why it boosts the performance of already powerful neodymium magnets.
Because electric cars need dysprosium-enhanced magnets, demand for this rare element has soared as EV production has grown.

image_caption: Holmium metal — a soft, malleable, silvery-white rare earth element

compounds.name: Holmium-doped YAG laser crystal
compounds.use: Powers surgical lasers used in kidney stone removal and eye surgery

compounds.name: Holmium oxide
compounds.use: Creates a yellow-orange colour in glass and cubic zirconia gemstones

facts.text: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any element — a single holmium atom on a surface can store one bit of data, making it a research target for ultimate-density data storage.
Holmium lasers are used by surgeons to break up kidney stones without any cutting — the laser is passed through a thin tube.
Holmium is named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm, Sweden.
In 2017, scientists demonstrated that a single holmium atom on a magnesium oxide surface could hold a stable magnetic state — the world's smallest magnet.

image_caption: Erbium metal — a silvery, soft rare earth that gives glass a pink colour when dissolved

compounds.name: Erbium ion in silica glass
compounds.use: Amplifies light signals in fibre optic cables — essential for the internet

compounds.name: Erbium oxide
compounds.use: Gives glass and ceramics a distinctive pink or rose colour

compounds.name: Erbium YAG laser
compounds.use: Used in skin resurfacing, dental drills, and eye surgery

facts.text: Almost every long-distance internet cable uses erbium-doped amplifiers — erbium ions in a tiny glass fibre boost the light signal every 80 km or so without converting it to electricity.
Erbium gives glass a delicate pink colour, which is why some decorative glasses and ceramics have a rosy tint.
Like terbium, erbium was named after the Swedish village of Ytterby where it was first found mixed with other rare earth minerals.
Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) were the breakthrough that made the modern high-speed internet possible in the 1990s.

image_caption: Thulium metal — one of the rarest and most expensive of the rare earth elements

compounds.name: Thulium YAG laser
compounds.use: Used in medical lasers for prostate treatment and kidney stone removal

compounds.name: Thulium oxide
compounds.use: Used in high-refractive-index glass for camera lenses

facts.text: Thulium is the second rarest naturally occurring element after promethium — global production is only a few tonnes per year.
Thulium is named after Thule, the ancient name for the far north of the world, probably referring to Scandinavia or Iceland.
Radioactive thulium-170 was once used in portable X-ray machines that required no electricity — useful in remote locations.
Thulium lasers operating around 2 micrometres are used in minimally invasive urology procedures because they cut tissue very precisely with minimal bleeding.

image_caption: Ytterbium metal — a soft, malleable silvery rare earth element

compounds.name: Ytterbium YAG laser
compounds.use: Powerful industrial lasers used for cutting and welding metal

compounds.name: Ytterbium oxide
compounds.use: Used in speciality glass and as a dopant in fibre lasers

facts.text: Ytterbium atoms are the heart of some of the most accurate clocks ever built — optical lattice clocks using ytterbium are so precise they would lose less than one second over the age of the universe.
Ytterbium is the fourth element named after Ytterby, Sweden — the same tiny village gave its name to yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium.
High-power ytterbium fibre lasers are used in factories to cut and weld steel, and are gradually replacing older carbon dioxide lasers.
Ytterbium's energy levels are so stable and narrow that atomic clocks based on it could detect tiny differences in gravity between floors of a building.

image_caption: Lutetium metal — the last and hardest of the lanthanide elements

compounds.name: Lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO)
compounds.use: Scintillator crystals in PET scanners used to detect cancer

compounds.name: Lutetium-177 peptide
compounds.use: Targeted radiation therapy for neuroendocrine tumours

facts.text: Lutetium-177 is one of the newest cancer treatments — it locks onto tumour cells and delivers radiation directly, sparing healthy tissue around them.
Lutetium is named after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris — it was discovered by a French chemist in 1907.
Lutetium is the densest and hardest of all the lanthanide elements, and it has the highest melting point in the group.
PET scanners — the machines that create 3D images to find cancer — use lutetium silicate crystals to detect the gamma rays produced inside your body.
Berkelium was first made in 1949 at the University of California, Berkeley, by bombarding americium-241 with alpha particles in a cyclotron.
It is named after Berkeley, California, just as its lighter cousin californium is named after the state itself.
Only microgram quantities of berkelium have ever been produced — it is so rare that a few millionths of a gram counts as a large sample.
Berkelium has no uses outside of scientific research, but it is used as a target material to synthesise even heavier elements higher up the periodic table.
Californium was first synthesised in 1950 at Berkeley by bombarding curium with alpha particles — making it the sixth transuranic element discovered.
Californium-252 is the most practical isotope: it spontaneously releases neutrons at an extraordinary rate, making a pellet the size of a pinhead a portable neutron source.
Tiny sources of californium-252 are used by oil companies to scan rock layers underground, and by airport security to detect explosives in luggage.
Californium is the heaviest element with a real-world application — all heavier elements are purely research curiosities made atom by atom.
Einsteinium was discovered in the radioactive debris of the first hydrogen bomb test — 'Ivy Mike' — in 1952. Its discovery was kept secret for years.
It is named after Albert Einstein, one of the greatest scientists in history and the author of E=mc², which describes how mass and energy are related.
Einsteinium is so intensely radioactive that a visible speck of it would glow in the dark and rapidly self-destruct from its own radiation.
In 2021, scientists finally measured some basic chemical properties of einsteinium for the first time, using samples containing just 200 billionths of a gram.
Fermium was also found in the fallout of the 1952 'Ivy Mike' hydrogen bomb test, discovered alongside einsteinium in the same classified investigation.
It is named after Enrico Fermi, the Italian-American physicist who built the world's first nuclear reactor under a sports stadium in Chicago in 1942.
Fermium is the heaviest element that can be produced by bombarding uranium with neutrons in a nuclear reactor — making heavier elements requires even more exotic methods.
Only tiny amounts of fermium have ever been made, and they exist for just days before decaying — it has no practical uses.
Mendelevium is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who created the periodic table in 1869 — without his work, we might never have known that elements like mendelevium should exist.
It was first made in 1955 by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles in a cyclotron at Berkeley — only 17 atoms were produced in the first experiment.
Being able to make just 17 atoms and still identify a new element was a triumph of nuclear chemistry and physics.
Mendelevium has no uses outside research; all its isotopes are radioactive and decay within weeks or months.
Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite and founded the Nobel Prizes — the most famous science awards in the world.
Its discovery in 1958–1966 was disputed for years between American and Soviet teams during the Cold War, each claiming to have made it first.
Nobelium was the first element to be discovered in the Soviet Union (at Dubna), though credit was eventually shared.
Nobelium's most stable isotope lasts only 58 minutes before decaying, and only a few atoms at a time have ever been produced.
Lawrencium is named after Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron particle accelerator — the type of machine used to create almost all synthetic elements.
It is the last actinide element, sitting directly below lutetium in the periodic table and completing the bottom row of the f-block.
Lawrencium was first made in 1961 at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory by bombarding californium with boron ions.
Only a few atoms of lawrencium are ever made at a time, and the longest-lived isotope decays in about 11 hours.
Rutherfordium is named after Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911 by shooting alpha particles at gold foil.
It is the first transactinide element — meaning it sits just after the actinides and begins a new section of the periodic table.
Rutherfordium is made by firing calcium ions at californium or plutonium targets in a particle accelerator; only a few atoms are produced per experiment.
Its most stable isotope, Rf-267, has a half-life of about 1.3 hours — long enough for scientists to study some of its basic chemistry before it vanishes.
Dubnium is named after Dubna, the Russian city that is home to the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR), where much of the early work on superheavy elements was done.
It was independently discovered by both American and Soviet scientists in the 1960s and 1970s, and the naming dispute lasted for decades during the Cold War.
Dubnium is created by colliding lighter nuclei together in a particle accelerator — for example, firing nitrogen ions at californium targets.
The longest-lived dubnium isotope has a half-life of about 28 hours — among the longest of any element this heavy.
Seaborgium is named after Glenn T. Seaborg, the American chemist who co-discovered ten elements — more than anyone else in history.
Seaborg was alive when element 106 was named after him in 1994, making him one of the only people honoured with an element name during their lifetime.
Seaborgium was first synthesised at Berkeley in 1974 by bombarding californium with oxygen ions in a heavy-ion linear accelerator.

Scientists have performed a few experiments showing seaborgium behaves chemically like tungsten, its lighter analogue in the periodic table — confirming the table's predictions even at extreme atomic numbers.
Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist who developed the first quantum model of the atom in 1913 and won the Nobel Prize in 1922.
It was first created in 1981 at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany, by bombarding bismuth-209 with chromium-54 ions.
Only a few dozen atoms of bohrium have ever been made; it decays in seconds to minutes depending on the isotope.
Despite its extreme rarity and short lifetime, chemists have managed to study bohrium's chemistry and confirmed it behaves like rhenium, as the periodic table predicts.
Hassium is named after Hassia, the Latin name for the German state of Hesse, where the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research (the lab that made it) is located.
It was first synthesised in 1984 at GSI by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg, who also discovered several other superheavy elements.
Hassium-270 has a half-life of about 9 seconds — remarkably long for an element this heavy, which allows scientists to study its chemistry.
Experiments show that hassium forms oxides that behave like osmium tetroxide, perfectly matching what the periodic table predicts for element 108.
Meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner, the Austrian-Swedish physicist who co-discovered nuclear fission in 1938 but was denied the Nobel Prize that her male collaborator received.
Meitnerium was first made in 1982 at GSI Darmstadt by fusing bismuth and iron nuclei together in an accelerator.
Only a handful of meitnerium atoms have ever existed; the most stable isotope decays in about 8 seconds.
Albert Einstein called Lise Meitner 'the most significant woman scientist of the 20th century' — naming element 109 after her is considered a long-overdue recognition.
Darmstadtium is named after Darmstadt, Germany — the city where GSI, the heavy-ion research centre that first created it in 1994, is located.
It was first made by firing nickel-62 ions at lead-208 targets; only a few atoms were produced in the initial experiment.
Darmstadtium's most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 11 seconds.
Elements this heavy sit in the periodic table's 6d transition metals, and scientists predict darmstadtium should behave somewhat like platinum — though almost no chemistry has been done on it.
Roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
It was first synthesised at GSI Darmstadt in 1994 by bombarding bismuth-209 with nickel-64 ions — only three atoms were detected.
Roentgenium's most stable known isotope lasts about 26 seconds before decaying.

Just as Röntgen's X-rays transformed medicine, roentgenium sits in a region of the periodic table where scientists hope to find exceptionally stable 'island of stability' isotopes in future experiments.
Copernicium is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, the Polish astronomer who first proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun rather than the other way around.
It was first created at GSI Darmstadt in 1996 by bombarding lead with zinc ions; only a handful of atoms have ever been made.
Scientists predict that copernicium may behave more like a noble gas than a metal at room temperature, because its electrons move so fast that relativistic effects become significant.
Some experiments suggest copernicium atoms interact very weakly with gold surfaces, hinting at noble-gas-like behaviour — though far fewer than a billion atoms of it have ever existed.
Nihonium's name comes from 'Nihon', which means 'Japan' in Japanese — it is the first element discovered in Asia and the first named in Japanese.
It was first created in 2004 at RIKEN, Japan's national research institute, by firing zinc ions at bismuth targets — it took nine years of experiments to confirm the discovery.
Nihonium was officially named in 2016, and the discovery was a source of enormous national pride in Japan.
Its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 20 seconds; only around 100 atoms of nihonium have ever been observed.

Flerovium is named after Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which was itself named after Georgy Flyorov — the Soviet physicist who sent a famous letter to Stalin arguing that Germany must be building an atomic bomb.
It was first synthesised in 1999 at Dubna by bombarding plutonium-244 with calcium-48 ions in a technique that has also produced several other superheavy elements.
Flerovium sits directly below lead in the periodic table, but relativistic quantum effects may make it behave more like a noble gas than a metal.
The most stable known isotope of flerovium has a half-life of about 2.1 seconds — one of the shorter-lived confirmed elements.
Moscovium is named after Moscow Oblast, the region in Russia that contains the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research at Dubna where it was created.
It was first synthesised in 2003 by a Russian-American collaboration, bombarding americium-243 with calcium-48 ions.
Only about 100 atoms of moscovium have ever been detected, and the most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 220 milliseconds.
Moscovium decays into nihonium (element 113), which was actually how nihonium was first discovered — as a decay product of moscovium.
Livermorium is named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in Livermore, California — one of the two institutions (along with Dubna) that co-discovered it.
It was first made in 2000 by bombarding curium-248 with calcium-48 ions at the Dubna accelerator facility.
Livermorium sits below polonium in the periodic table, and scientists predict it may behave somewhat like a very heavy version of polonium — though far more unstable.
The most stable known isotope of livermorium decays in about 61 milliseconds — less than a tenth of a second after it is born.
Tennessine is named after Tennessee, USA — honouring Vanderbilt University, the University of Tennessee, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory, all of which contributed to its discovery.
It was first created in 2010 at Dubna by a Russian-American team, bombarding berkelium-249 with calcium-48 ions.
Tennessine is the second-heaviest element ever confirmed; only a few dozen atoms of it have ever been detected, each surviving for only milliseconds.
Despite being placed in the halogen column of the periodic table (below astatine), tennessine is predicted to behave very differently from fluorine or chlorine due to extreme relativistic effects.
Oganesson is the heaviest element on the periodic table — element 118 — and it sits in the noble gas column, though scientists think it may actually be a solid at room temperature rather than a gas.

It is named after Yuri Oganessian, a Russian nuclear physicist who pioneered the technique of using calcium-48 beams to create superheavy elements — he is one of the very few living people to have an element named after them.
Only five atoms of oganesson have ever been detected, each surviving for less than a millisecond before decaying.
Oganesson was first synthesised in 2002 at Dubna by bombarding californium-249 with calcium-48 ions, and its discovery was confirmed in 2006.
